comments.text:
Developers code their games to run on a particular vendor's architecture.  AMD is a more paralleled architecture while NVidia's is more traditional sequential/serial in manner.  AMD's is theoretically more efficient because cheaper paralleled GPU's can be made with similar performance to sequential GPU's.  However, paralleled GPU's require more API support, otherwise much of it goes unused.  This is why AMD catches up in Vulkan and DX12 games, because the API works better on AMD.

NVidia is going to have a harder time convincing developers to optimize for their cards because the API's exist for easy console to PC ports for AMD hardware.  If one takes into account all gaming GPU's (Console + PC), AMD outnumbers NVidia something like 6:1.  It doesn't make much sense for developers to spend time optimizing for NVidia GPU's anymore.  A PC user isn't worth anymore to a developer than a console user.

NVidia's cards are specifically designed for gaming, while AMD favors compute performance.  AMD tends to be more all-around, for things like video editing and encoding.

NVidia may have more PC marketshare, but it doesn't really matter.  Developers wanted easier porting and more hardware control, and this was given to them with DX12 and Vulkan/Mantle.  AMD worked closely with Microsoft on DX12, and AMD's Mantle was given to Khronos to make Vulkan.  AMD has worked their fingers into the API's.  It's not so much that NVidia hardware will lose performance, but rather AMD's will gain and force NVidia to cut prices.
